Non-tidal water level changes, in centimeters

An attempt at a live(-ish) coastal investigation

Can we watch a Kelvin wave move up the California coast?

NOAA collects tide data along the California coastline. I wanted to see if tide gauges might show Kelvin waves moving along the coast.

Scroll to investigate ↓

Step 01

Kelvin waves aren't just another wave. They're disturbances that can travel along coastlines, affecting sea level and sometimes the structure of the water below.

Below, each line is an observed water level at a station, minus the tide prediction for that location.

According to their Wiki, surface-level Kelvins can move very fast. The internal waves (bringing warm water) travel at a slower pace.

What's happening daily?

Residual water levels, by day.

Step 02

Looking at the daily cells in an attempt to make broader shifts up the coast visible.

Color is scaled to the loaded observations. If there's not enough data per day, it shows as "missing" and is dark/empty.

Step 02 / A closer read

They're ordered by their distance from San Diego moving north.

A coordinated sea level change should (maybe) arrive progressively later as it travels north. Similar patterns may suggest it, but we can't assume it.

The next chart gets more granular in 3-hour station measurements around a station's peak water level.

Zoom in: Looking closer at coastal candidates

Do the dates line up? Will this show something useful?

Step 03

Reading the latest observed days.

Each strip is a station's own measurements. The lines identifies a potential candidate peak from the southern reference gauge. The circles highlight the neighboring measured bins with similar heights.

Still not a clear sign of a Kelvin wave.

Step 03 / The question

Do similar changes show up farther north later, in a way that suggests they could be related?

The full dashboard keeps the coverage and lag tests alongside this visual check.

Zoom out: Off-shore satellite measures

What changed offshore?

04

Copernicus satellite data adds a broader offshore reading. It's mentioned as a more common way to show/find our coastal Kelvin. Each block shows how much higher or lower the satellite-estimated sea level is compared with the average for the area over the previous seven days.

These pull in large 0.125° gridded samples (12-14 km area) and sit further offshore. They're more likely to show changes in sea level of the slower, warm Kelvin. It provides context for better understanding the above coastal gauges (but not a substitute).

04 / An overhead view

Similar to above, the satellite rows are offshore grid-cell estimates, not the tide-gauge measurements. I included them to show whether broader sea-level change is visible beyond the coastline.

Conclusion (so far)

Still looking for a clear signal. What would you try next? Any tips on how to improve detection – Sea Surface Temperature? Other stations? Other data?
